questions.questionText: Write a formal letter to your school head requesting a school vegetable garden. Explain its benefits and how it could be maintained.
questions.explanation:
**Formal Letter Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Use **Two-Address Formal Letter Format**: top right carries your own school address and date; left margin below carries *The Head, [School Name], P.O. Box ...*; followed by **"Dear Sir/Madam,"** and a bold underlined subject line (**RE: REQUEST TO ESTABLISH A SCHOOL VEGETABLE GARDEN**). **Paragraph 1:** Politely introduce yourself on behalf of the Grade 7 Environmental/Agriculture Club and state the clear purpose of requesting a fenced unused corner plot behind the classrooms for a vegetable bed project.

**Paragraph 2 (Benefits & Sustainability):** Explain three concrete benefits cleanly—producing fresh covo, tomatoes, and onions to enrich school feeding meals (*nutritious balanced diet*), giving learners hands-on **Agric, Science & Technology** practice in composting, mulching, and *Pfumvudza* water conservation, and raising small income from surplus bunches for stationery/tools. 

**Paragraph 3 (Maintenance Plan & Formal Sign-Off):** Reassure the Head with a structured maintenance rota (morning watering rosters before assembly, rabbit/chicken wire fencing using club contributions, natural ash/marigold pest control, and teacher supervision during holidays), ending respectfully with **"Yours faithfully,"** and your full name.

Never omit the second (recipient’s) address or forget the **RE:** heading line, and always keep formal polite phrasing (*"I humbly request...", "We guarantee..."*)—never informal chat or *"Yours affectionately."*

questions.questionText: Write a composition about a day when you helped a stranger. Describe what happened, how you helped and what you learnt.
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Structure **"A day when I helped a stranger"** into four focused chronological paragraphs using vivid past-tense English. **Paragraph 1 (Meeting & Problem):** Set a believable Saturday morning scene—walking home from market shops or waiting at a rural clinic—when you notice an elderly stranger or worried young mother in genuine need (e.g., an elderly gogo’s heavy sack split open scattering maize meal across gravel, or a lost tourist searching for the main clinic).

**Paragraph 2 (Action & Kindness):** Describe step-by-step how you stepped in respectfully without expecting payment: kneeling swiftly to scoop clean grain into your spare shopping bag, carrying her load safely along the dusty path to the bus rank, or guiding a visitor politely to the duty nurse while offering cool drinking water. 

**Paragraph 3 (Gratitude & Lesson Learnt):** Capture the stranger’s genuine thankfulness and reflect clearly on what the moment taught you about ***Unhu/Ubuntu***, courage, and noticing quiet neighbours in need—making small acts of helpfulness deeply rewarding.

**Examiner Guidance:** Avoid far-fetched superhero rescues; ZIMSEC Grade 7 markers reward warm, everyday realistic kindness told with crisp sensory details and clean past-tense verb control.

questions.questionText: Write a speech encouraging learners to protect trees around the school. Give at least three practical actions.
questions.explanation:
**Speech Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Open with a clear formal assembly greeting: *"The School Head, respected teachers, and dear fellow learners, good morning."* **Paragraph 1 (Importance of Trees):** State your persuasive theme immediately—trees are the green lungs of our school, giving cool study shade during scorching October afternoons, sheltering birds, anchoring soil against heavy gully erosion, and enriching fresh oxygen.

**Paragraph 2 (Three Practical Learner Actions):** Present three specific actions pupils can start today: **(1) Adopt-a-Sapling Teams**, where each class plants and waters one hardy indigenous or fruit tree (guava, acacia, msasa) with mulch basins around the roots; **(2) Protect Young Bark & Branches**, strictly stopping swinging on saplings, carving initials into trunks, or breaking live twigs for play; and **(3) Practise Paper Recycling & Clean Firewood Habits**, cutting wasteful exercise-book tearing and clearing dry dead branches responsibly instead of cutting living trees. 

**Paragraph 3 (Closing Challenge):** Remind peers that *"One learner, one thriving tree"* transforms bare dusty yards into green legacy gardens, closing politely with **"Thank you very much."**

Remember speech voice uses **"we", "us", "let us"** directly toward live listeners—avoid turning a speech into a silent essay or writing letter addresses.

questions.questionText: Write a report to your head teacher about a lost-and-found incident at school. Include the time, place, action taken and recommendations.
questions.explanation:
**School Lost-and-Found Report Guide [20 marks]:** Format strictly as an official **ZIMSEC Report**: **TO:** The Head Teacher | **FROM:** [Your Full Name, Grade 7 Prefect] | **DATE:** [Date] | **SUBJECT:** Report on Lost-and-Found Sports Bag Incident. **Paragraph 1 (Time, Place & Discovery):** State factually that on Wednesday afternoon around 1:15 p.m. near the Grade 6 bicycle shed, you spotted an unattended navy backpack containing a calculator, ZIMSEC revision book, and $15 in an envelope.

**Paragraph 2 (Action Taken):** Detail transparent, honest custody steps taken immediately: without opening pockets further, you left the bag untouched in content, asked fellow monitor Tariro to witness the hand-over, delivered the bag safely to the Senior Teacher on Duty’s locked office, logged a brief item description in the school lost-property register, and watched assembly announcement verify the rightful Grade 5 owner cleanly the next morning. 

**Paragraph 3 (Recommendations):** Propose two clear preventative measures—labelling all bags and stationery clearly with permanent markers at term start, and placing a dedicated lockable Lost-and-Found cabinet near reception—signed formally *"Submitted by [Full Name]"*.

Keep report language calm, factual, third-person/objective, and strictly in past tense—never add casual greetings or *"Yours sincerely."*

questions.questionText: Describe a memorable visit to a tourist attraction in Zimbabwe. Include the journey, what you saw and what you learnt.
questions.explanation:
**Descriptive Composition Guide — Visiting a Zimbabwean Tourist Attraction [20 marks]:** Pick a real national treasure you can describe richly—such as **Victoria Falls (*Mosi-oa-Tunya*)**, **Great Zimbabwe Ruins**, **Matobo Hills**, **Nyanga Mountains**, or **Chinhoyi Caves**. **Paragraph 1 (The Journey):** Set out at dawn by school bus or family car, capturing changing rural landscapes, acacia hills, cheerful songs onboard, and mounting excitement as welcome signposts appear.

**Paragraph 2 (What You Saw & Experienced):** Paint vivid sensory details—the rising white mist and roaring thunder of Victoria Falls soaking visitors along Rainforest walkways, or monumental dry-stone granite enclosures climbing hills at Great Zimbabwe—alongside knowledgeable guides explaining indigenous heritage and local woodcarvers’ markets. 

**Paragraph 3 (What You Learnt):** Conclude thoughtfully explaining what you discovered about Zimbabwe’s geological wonders, pre-colonial engineering, wildlife conservation, and why tourism jobs require every citizen to protect natural shrines from litter and vandalism.

Include **accurate local geographic details** and crisp sensory imagery (sound, mist, granite colour, birdsong) rather than generic statements like *"it was very nice and we ate food."*

questions.questionText: Write an informal letter to a relative thanking them for helping you with your school work.
questions.explanation:
**Informal Letter Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Use **Single-Address Friendly Format** (your own home/school address + date at top right; warm greeting *"Dear Auntie Rudo,"* or *"Dear Uncle Farai,"* on the left). **Paragraph 1 (Warm Greeting & Reason):** Ask kindly after your relative’s health and family, then immediately state your heartfelt purpose—writing to express sincere gratitude for the patient evening coaching in Mathematics fractions and buying your Grade 7 Science revision pack.

**Paragraph 2 (Impact & Progress):** Describe clearly how their patient encouragement boosted your confidence: share a specific improvement—jumping from 54% to 82% in mock paper tests, mastering long division without panic, and helping younger siblings read aloud nicely at home—showing their sacrifice truly bore fruit. 

**Paragraph 3 (Update & Warm Sign-off):** Promise to keep working diligently toward top Grade 7 ZIMSEC results, share brief joyful news of school activities, and close affectionately with *"Your grateful niece/nephew, [First Name only]."*

Match warm respectful family tone suited to an elder relative (*Uncle/Auntie*)—courteous and grateful without slang like *"Hey bro!"* or overly stiff business words like *"Yours faithfully."*

questions.questionText: Write a story beginning: 'The moment the lights went out, everyone became silent.'
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Open **verbatim** with: **"The moment the lights went out, everyone became silent."** **Paragraph 1 (Setting & Instant Tension):** Establish a quiet evening scene—say, evening Grade 7 boarding study prep or a stormy night indoors watching the end of a family story—when thunder snaps overhead and pitch darkness floods every corner of the hall simultaneously.

**Paragraph 2 (Action & Resolution):** Describe believable physical reactions in the dark—chairs scraping softly, someone fumbling calmly for a solar lantern/torch, a prefect reassuring younger peers to stay seated safely rather than rushing doorways in panic, and the glowing warm beam of candles turning anxious tension into cheerful calm conversation or singing while rain taps roof iron. 

**Paragraph 3 (Return of Power & Reflection):** When solar/power clicks back warmly twenty minutes later, show everyone laughing kindly and concluding what staying calm under sudden surprises taught the group about teamwork and level-headedness.

**Examiner Guidance:** Never rely on cheap horror ghosts or waking from a dream—grounded realistic human reactions earn the highest ZIMSEC Content and Style scores.

questions.questionText: Write a speech to be delivered at assembly about the importance of punctuality.
questions.explanation:
**Assembly Speech Guide — Importance of Punctuality [20 marks]:** Begin properly: *"The Head, Deputy Head, teachers, and fellow learners, good morning."* **Paragraph 1 (Hook & Definition):** Explain crisply what **punctuality** means—arriving on time before the morning bell, submitting homework promptly, and honouring scheduled lessons—before asking what happens when one latecomer bursts noisily into class mid-lesson.

**Paragraph 2 (Three Reasons Punctuality Matters):** Develop **(1) Respect for Others’ Time**—interrupting morning devotions or Mathematics instructions steals learning minutes from forty waiting classmates; **(2) Building Academic Calm & Success**—settling desks five minutes early prevents rushed forgotten pens and exam panic; and **(3) Preparing Future Character**—doctors, drivers, farmers, and engineers depend daily on reliability and self-discipline. 

**Paragraph 3 (Action Plan):** Encourage practical morning habits—packing satchels and polishing uniforms the night before and setting out fifteen minutes early—ending warmly with **"Thank you for your attention."**

Write rhythmically as spoken persuasion (*"Look around your morning desk...", "Let us start tomorrow..."*) so the assembly speech reads convincingly aloud.

questions.questionText: Write a report about a sports day held at your school. Include activities, participation, results and recommendations.
questions.explanation:
**Sports Day Report Guide [20 marks]:** Structure clearly with formal header (**TO: The Head Teacher | FROM: [Your Full Name, Sports Secretary] | DATE: [Date] | SUBJECT: Report on the Annual Inter-House School Sports Day**). **Paragraph 1 (Overview & Participation):** Log date, venue, participating houses (e.g., *Eagle, Lion, Buffalo, Kudu*), turnout of parents/community, and smooth opening march-past.

**Paragraph 2 (Activities & Official Results):** Summarise key track/field disciplines cleanly (sprints, relays, long jump, netball/football friendlies) alongside crisp factual outcomes—for example, *Kudu House captured 1st place overall with 385 points, closely followed by Eagle House (360 points); Grade 7 relay teams recorded strong sportsmanship with zero disqualifications*. 

**Paragraph 3 (Observations & Recommendations):** Note two strengths (enthusiastic participation, prompt first-aid support) plus two practical improvements for next year (re-marking faded lane chalk earlier and adding extra shaded water jugs at the finish line), signed professionally at bottom.

**Examiner Guidance:** Maintain crisp factual past-tense reporting—keep personal boasting out and balance praise fairly with practical logistical recommendations.

questions.questionText: Write a composition explaining how your community can prepare for floods.
questions.explanation:
**Expository Composition Guide — Preparing Your Community for Floods [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (Introduction):** Define seasonal **flash floods and river overflows** caused by heavy Cyclone or summer cloudbursts across Zimbabwe, stating clearly that early community planning saves human lives, livestock, and precious harvests.

**Paragraph 2 (Three Practical Preparation Measures):** Explain **(1) Clearing Storm Drains, Culverts & Waterways** before October rains so rushing runoff flows harmlessly instead of bursting into homes; **(2) Relocating Homes/Kraals Away from Low River Floodplains & Elevating Grain/Seed Stores** onto raised brick platforms above damp flood lines while storing waterproof emergency kits (torches, dry food, clinic records, water-purification tablets); and **(3) Community Early-Warning Alerts & Safe Evacuation Routes** where village heads/schools share weather bulletins and rehearse moving children, elders, and cattle to high ground *before* rivers rise dangerously.

**Paragraph 3 (Conclusion — Golden Rule & Unity):** Conclude urgently with the lifesaving rule **"Never cross flooded low-level bridges or fast brown rivers on foot or by bus"**, showing how disciplined cooperation protects whole villages through storm seasons.

questions.questionText: Write a formal letter to a local organisation requesting support for a school reading club.
questions.explanation:
**Formal Letter Plan — Requesting Reading Club Support [20 marks]:** Apply strict **Two-Address Formal Format** (your school’s address/date top right; left margin recipient address e.g., *The Director, [Local Business / Book Trust], Harare*; **"Dear Sir/Madam,"**; bold subject heading **RE: REQUEST FOR BOOK DONATION SUPPORT FOR OUR SCHOOL READING CLUB**). **Paragraph 1:** Introduce your school’s newly launched 40-member Reading Club respectfully, explaining learners’ keen hunger to improve English comprehension and general knowledge despite severe shortages of age-appropriate storybooks.

**Paragraph 2 (Specific Need & Impact):** Specify exactly what support would help—used or new primary storybooks, encyclopedias, ZIMSEC reference dictionaries, or sturdy wooden shelves—and illustrate clearly how 100 shared books can rotate cleanly among all Grade 5–7 classes during lunch breaks and weekend reading circles, lifting literacy scores and protecting youths from idle habits. 

**Paragraph 3 (Accountability & Polite Close):** Promise careful book-lending tracking, protective plastic book covers, and a termly thank-you progress letter before closing formally with **"Yours faithfully,"**, signature, and full printed name.

questions.questionText: Write a story about a mistake that taught you an important lesson.
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan — A Mistake That Taught an Important Lesson [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (Situation & Poor Choice):** Introduce a realistic mistake driven by impatience or carelessness—for instance, rushing out to play football before locking the backyard chicken coop or copying a friend’s homework/ignoring an adult safety rule about cycling without working brakes.

**Paragraph 2 (Immediate Consequence):** Describe vividly what went wrong when that shortcut backfired—stray dogs frightening prized hens, or skidding awkwardly onto a gravel verge grazing your knee and bending the front wheel—highlighting panic, regret, and honest embarrassment as family members rushed to help fix the damage cleanly. 

**Paragraph 3 (Lesson & Changed Behaviour):** Show yourself apologising sincerely, helping repair the mess/earn back trust over the following weeks, and ending thoughtfully with how one painful afternoon taught lasting responsibility (*measuring consequences before acting in haste*).

**Examiner Guidance:** Remember: strong narratives examine *why* the mistake happened, genuine feelings afterward, and concrete growth—not merely *"I made a mistake, sorry, the end."*

questions.questionText: Write a speech welcoming visitors to your school and describing its achievements.
questions.explanation:
**Welcome Speech Guide — Welcoming Visitors & Describing School Achievements [20 marks]:** Open warmly: *"The Guest of Honour, School Head, parents, visiting educators, teachers, and fellow learners, warm greetings and a hearty welcome to [School Name]."* **Paragraph 1 (Welcome Hospitality):** Extend proud Zimbabwean hospitality (*"Makorokoto / Siyalemukela"* spirit), thanking guests warmly for sparing valuable time to tour the classrooms and encourage young learners.

**Paragraph 2 (School Achievements Showcase):** Highlight 3–4 authentic pride points concisely—consistent Grade 7 ZIMSEC pass rates led by dedicated staff, thriving **Pfumvudza** vegetable beds feeding healthy lunches, gleaming trophies in girls’ netball/traditional marimba competitions, and clean solar-lit computer/reading corners built through strong parent–teacher partnership. 

**Paragraph 3 (Closing Invitation):** Invite visitors happily to inspect learner art displays and join afternoon refreshments, ending courteously with **"Once again, feel warmly at home—thank you!"**

questions.questionText: Write a report about an incident in which a learner prevented an accident at school.
questions.explanation:
**Accident-Prevention Incident Report Guide [20 marks]:** Begin with strict **Report Header** (**TO:** The Head Teacher | **FROM:** [Name, Grade 7 Safety Prefect] | **DATE:** [Date] | **SUBJECT:** Report on Swift Prevention of Electrical/Playground Hazard near Block B). **Paragraph 1 (Time & Hazard Identified):** Record concisely what happened: on Tuesday 10:15 a.m. during mid-morning break, Grade 7 learner *Farai Banda* noticed a bare frayed extension cord sparking beside a puddle outside the tuckshop / or noticed younger children climbing an unstable broken goalpost / sharp broken bottle hidden in grass.

**Paragraph 2 (Swift Protective Action):** Describe objective step-by-step response: Farai immediately shouted calmly to halt running peers well back from the wet cord/broken frame, stationed a friend to keep curious Grade 2s clear, and sprinted directly to alert the Deputy Head and caretaker, who isolated the mains breaker/barricaded the goal cleanly before a single child was shocked or injured. 

**Paragraph 3 (Recommendations):** Praise Farai’s alert citizenship and recommend weekly visual safety sweeps of electrical cords and outdoor equipment before break times, closing professionally.

questions.questionText: Describe the busiest market you have visited. Include sights, sounds, people and goods.
questions.explanation:
**Descriptive Composition — The Busiest Market Visited [20 marks]:** Capture an unforgettable Zimbabwean market scene (like **Mbare Musika**, **Sakubva**, or a vibrant rural growth-point Saturday market) across rich sensory details. **Paragraph 1 (Sight & Colour):** Paint bustling wooden stalls overflowing with pyramids of glossy red tomatoes, emerald green covo bundles, golden mangoes, neatly woven reed baskets, and vibrant chitenge fabrics fluttering above narrow bustling aisles.

**Paragraph 2 (Sound, Smell & Hustle):** Bring the air alive with lively sounds and scents—cheerful vendors calling competitive prices (*"Two dollars for a fresh bucket!"*), pushcart porters whistling *"Pachedu, move gently!"*, roasting sweet green mealies mingling with ripe guavas and damp morning dust, and shoppers bargaining good-humouredly while tucking goods into striped bags. 

**Paragraph 3 (Human Atmosphere & Conclusion):** Reflect warmly on the tireless energy of hard-working traders sustaining families from dawn till dusk—an unforgettable symphony of Zimbabwean enterprise and community warmth.

questions.questionText: Write an informal letter to a friend explaining how you prepared for an important examination.
questions.explanation:
**Informal Letter Plan — Exam Preparation Advice to a Friend [20 marks]:** Format cleanly with **one top-right address + date**, left salutation (*"Dear Tinashe,"*), warm opening checking on their revision progress before sharing practical ZIMSEC exam preparation habits that worked brilliantly for you.

**Paragraph 2 (Actionable Study Strategies):** Share 3 concrete study methods warmly—making a balanced **daily revision timetable** dividing tricky weak topics (like fractions and grammar) from confident subjects; **practising past Paper 1 & Paper 2 timed mocks** with honest self-marking against official mark schemes; and forming quiet afternoon **study pairs** to quiz each other aloud plus sleeping early for sharp morning recall. 

**Paragraph 3 (Encouragement & Friendly Sign-off):** Wish Tinashe calm confidence on exam morning—advising reading questions carefully twice without panicking—and close affectionately (*"Your best friend, Nyasha."*).

questions.questionText: Write a story ending: 'From that day onwards, I never ignored good advice.'
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition — Ending "...never ignored good advice." [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (The Ignored Warning):** Begin with a trusted adult or wise friend giving clear, kind advice—for instance, *"Wear your rain jacket and stay off the slippery clay shortcut beside the gully before the storm breaks"* or *"Double-check your bicycle chain and pack early before the trip."* Impatiently brushing it aside lands you in swift trouble.

**Paragraph 2 (The Crisis Unfolding):** Describe step-by-step the consequence of ignoring caution—sliding halfway down muddy banks ruining clean shoes and dropping schoolbooks in drizzle, or running out of supplies miles from home—feeling silly and humbled as a rescuer helps pull you safely back up. 

**Paragraph 3 (Wise Turnaround & Exact Closing Line):** Reflect on thanking your adviser honestly afterward and close word-for-word with the required prompt sentence: **"From that day onwards, I never ignored good advice."**

questions.questionText: Write a persuasive speech explaining why learners should reduce littering.
questions.explanation:
**Persuasive Speech — Reducing Littering at School [20 marks]:** Open firmly: *"The Head, teachers, and fellow learners, good morning."* **Paragraph 1 (Shocking Reality & Urgency):** Point politely toward stray sweet wrappers, broken plastic pens, and juice bottles scattered near playing fields despite visible dustbins—asking whether any of us would happily throw garbage onto our own bedroom floor at home.

**Paragraph 2 (Three Reasons & Practical Steps):** Convince peers clearly that **(1) Litter harms soil, animals, and drains** (clogging stormwater pipes and choking goats or cows that swallow crisp packets); **(2) Dirty grounds breed flies and embarrassment** when visitors inspect our school; and **(3) Every learner can act simply**: pocket wrappers until reaching a bin, reuse sturdy water bottles instead of single-use sachets, and remind friends gently (*"Bin it, don’t drop it!"*). 

**Paragraph 3 (Inspiring Close):** Call for every class to keep a zero-litter zone outside its doorway, closing with **"Together we keep our school shining—thank you!"**

questions.questionText: Write a report on a school clean-up campaign.
questions.explanation:
**School Clean-Up Campaign Report Guide [20 marks]:** Open with **Report Header**: **TO:** The Head Teacher / Environmental Committee | **FROM:** [Full Name, Health Club Chairperson] | **DATE:** [Date] | **SUBJECT:** Report on Friday National School Clean-Up Campaign. **Paragraph 1 (Time, Scope & Attendance):** Detail when all Grade 4–7 learners, teachers, and parent representatives gathered (Friday morning 8:00–10:30 a.m.) equipped with gloves, rakes, sacks, and brooms.

**Paragraph 2 (Work Accomplished):** Report clearly how zones were divided cleanly—sweeping tarmac walkways, separating collected plastic bottles from biodegradable dry leaves into the garden compost pit, scrubbing toilets and taps with disinfectant, and unblocking storm trenches behind classrooms before washing hands safely with soap. 

**Paragraph 3 (Outcome & Recommendations):** Note the spotless visual transformation alongside two recommendations—adding two covered bins near the tuckshop and awarding a monthly "Cleanest Class Shield" to sustain daily tidiness—signed cleanly.

questions.questionText: Explain how a family can save water during a dry season.
questions.explanation:
**Expository Essay — How a Family Can Save Water During a Dry Season [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (Urgency & Theme):** Define dry-season water scarcity (falling borehole tables and low dam levels between May and October), stating clearly that wise household water conservation keeps drinking supplies lasting until early summer rains return.

**Paragraph 2 (Practical Conservation Methods):** Detail three proven domestic savings habits cleanly: **(1) Repairing dripping taps, leaky joints, and overflowing toilet cisterns immediately**, stopping thousands of lost litres every month; **(2) Practising Greywater Reuse & Efficient Washing**—using a basin instead of a running hosepipe to wash dishes and cars, then pouring clean soapy rinse water carefully around fruit trees and banana basins; and **(3) Morning/Evening Garden Mulching & Bucket Watering**, applying dry grass mulch so soil retains cool moisture overnight instead of midday hose evaporation. 

**Paragraph 3 (Conclusion):** Emphasise closing taps tightly between scrubbing soap and teaching young siblings that *"Every conserved drop keeps our household healthy and green."*'

questions.questionText: Write a formal complaint to a bus company about unsafe passenger behaviour on a school route.
questions.explanation:
**Formal Letter of Complaint Guide [20 marks]:** Use strict **Two-Address Formal Format**: your home/school address & date top right; *The Transport Manager, [Bus Company Name], [City]* on left margin; **"Dear Sir/Madam,"**; and bold heading **RE: COMPLAINT REGARDING UNSAFE PASSENGER CONDUCT ON MORNING SCHOOL ROUTE**. **Paragraph 1:** State politely yet firmly the exact route, time (e.g., 6:45 a.m. weekday Chitungwiza–CBD service), and unsafe incidents witnessed (overcrowding passengers standing on steps with open moving doors, loud aggressive behaviour pushing small pupils, and drivers ignoring safe zebra-crossing stops).

**Paragraph 2 (Safety Risk & Urgent Request):** Explain calmly why these practices endanger school learners’ lives—especially risk of children falling onto tarmac when braking suddenly—and request three concrete company fixes: limiting boarding strictly to seated/safe standing capacity, closing doors securely before moving, and assigning a responsible conductor to uphold courteous passenger discipline. 

**Paragraph 3 (Professional Close):** Request an urgent review and written reply before closing formally with **"Yours faithfully,"** and full name.

questions.questionText: Write a story about a school trip that did not go according to plan but ended successfully.
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition — School Trip Turned Successful [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (High Hopes & Unexpected Hitch):** Describe excited departure for a Grade 7 science/history excursion (e.g., visiting Chinhoyi Caves or a botanical farm) before an unexpected setback strikes—such as a punctured rear coach tyre miles from town or sudden heavy downpour washing out the planned outdoor picnic pavilion.

**Paragraph 2 (Resourcefulness & Teamwork):** Show calm teachers and creative learners adapting positively instead of complaining—organising cheerful quizzes and folk songs under safe shelter, helping distribute dry raincoats/sandwiches cleanly while mechanics change the wheel smoothly, or turning a rainy morning into an unforgettable guided indoor museum & rock-art workshop where everyone asked thoughtful questions. 

**Paragraph 3 (Triumphant Finish):** Describe returning home laughing after sunshine returned cleanly over an extended afternoon tour, concluding how patience and teamwork rescued the day brilliantly.

questions.questionText: Write a speech encouraging young people to value traditional culture while respecting other cultures.
questions.explanation:
**Speech — Valuing Traditional Culture While Respecting Others [20 marks]:** Greet warmly: *"Honoured guests, teachers, parents, and fellow youths, good morning."* **Paragraph 1 (Identity Roots):** Celebrate Zimbabwe’s rich indigenous traditions—respecting elders with *Unhu/Ubuntu*, joyful *mbira* and *ngoma* rhythms, proverbs (*tsumo*), traditional attire, and communal *nhimbe* solidarity—which anchor our confidence and belonging in a fast-modernising world.

**Paragraph 2 (Respecting Diversity):** Urge young citizens equally to welcome neighbours’ diverse heritages without mocking accents, regional languages (*ChiShona, IsiNdebele, Kalanga, Tonga, Venda, Nambya*), foods, or religious customs. Compare society to a magnificent multi-coloured woven basket (*tswanda*): every unique strand strengthens the whole pattern only when woven side-by-side in mutual respect rather than pride or prejudice. 

**Paragraph 3 (Closing Appeal):** Challenge youths to preserve mother-tongue songs proudly while learning polite greetings across neighbouring cultures—ending **"Respect every root, honour one united nation. Thank you."**

questions.questionText: Write a report about a tree-planting event held in your community.
questions.explanation:
**Community Tree-Planting Report Guide [20 marks]:** Format with **TO: The Ward Councillor / Head Teacher | FROM: [Your Name, Youth Conservation Representative] | DATE: [Date] | SUBJECT: Report on National Tree-Planting Day Event**. **Paragraph 1 (Overview):** State clearly the Saturday morning date, location (around the clinic perimeter and stream buffer), participants (learners, Forestry Commission officers, village elders), and total trees planted (e.g., 120 indigenous *musasa*, *muhacha*, and mango/guava seedlings).

**Paragraph 2 (Activities & Aftercare Plan):** Detail accurate preparation steps observed—digging deep compost-enriched holes 3 metres apart, soaking basins cleanly, wrapping thorn/wire mesh cages to shield young stems from wandering goats, and registering community volunteers for bi-weekly dry-season watering. 

**Paragraph 3 (Assessment & Recommendations):** Conclude positively on strong community enthusiasm alongside recommending two follow-up actions (monthly survival checks after six months and mulching around saplings before winter winds), signed neatly.

questions.questionText: Describe a person who has influenced your education and explain why that person is important to you.
questions.explanation:
**Descriptive Person Portrait — Educational Mentor [20 marks]:** Choose someone genuinely inspiring—such as an encouraging Grade 5 teacher (*Mr Ncube*), a tireless elder sister, or a grandmother who read by lantern light. **Paragraph 1 (Introduction & Physical Presence):** Introduce their role in your life and paint warm physical character details—bright alert eyes, tidy chalk-dusted cardigan or neatly braided hair, calm steady posture, and the unhurried kindness in their smile.

**Paragraph 2 (Personality & Educational Influence):** Illustrate *specifically* how they shaped your learning—staying thirty minutes after bell time to walk patiently through long division on scrap chalkboards without scolding mistakes, lending personal storybooks cleanly wrapped in brown paper, and praising small daily effort rather than perfection alone. 

**Paragraph 3 (Lasting Impact):** Reflect warmly on carrying their calm habits (*"Never quit before trying three different ways"*) into your own Grade 7 exam preparation and daily kindness toward younger learners.

questions.questionText: What is the main idea of the passage?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** The **main idea** of a passage states the **central overarching message or purpose that links every paragraph together from beginning to end**—typically identified by combining the opening paragraph’s topic introduction with the concluding paragraph’s final outcome or lesson (avoid copying just one minor example from the middle!).

To verify you captured the true main idea rather than a minor supporting detail, summarise the passage silently in one clear sentence covering **Who / What topic**, **What key problem or action occurred**, and **Why it mattered**. Every supporting paragraph should fit neatly underneath that umbrella sentence like branches under one trunk.

In ZIMSEC Grade 7 Paper 2 Comprehension, examiners subtract marks if answers are overly vague (*"It is about good things"*) or copy a random middle quote. State one crisp, complete sentence naming the **exact central subject and primary outcome** from the text.

questions.questionText: What problem or need led to the activity?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** Identifying **"what problem or need led to the activity"** requires scanning Paragraph 1 or 2 of the given passage for **negative warning cues or gaps**—words such as *shortage, broken, dirty, flooded, lacked, struggled, complained, or neglected*—that pushed characters or the community to organise the activity described later.

Always pair the exact root problem directly from the text in your **own clean, grammatical sentence** (for example: *"The activity began because learners lacked clean reading space and shelves in the hall were broken"*) rather than pasting unrelated positive outcomes from later paragraphs.

Notice the #1 national Grade 7 error on *"What need led to..."* questions: candidates accidentally write the *solution* (*"They raised money to buy trees"*) instead of the *initial shortage/problem* (*"Severe soil erosion had washed away school footpaths"*). Answer strictly *why it started*!

questions.questionText: Which statement is supported by the passage?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** Verifying **which statement is supported by the passage** demands matching each detail strictly against written evidence inside the text without guessing or adding outside opinions from memory. An acceptable supported statement agrees completely with names, numbers, causes, and time order stated directly by the author.

When selecting or constructing a supported statement in Paper 2, scan back line-by-line to locate the exact supporting sentence and beware subtle **distortions**—such as swapping *"some"* with *"all"*, shifting past actions into future claims, or mixing up which character performed which job.

Write your answer in a clear declarative full sentence (*"The passage explicitly shows that [exact evidence from paragraph X]"*), checking spelling of any proper names lifted from the text.

questions.questionText: What lesson can be learnt?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** Extracting **"what lesson can be learnt"** tests higher-order inference: translate the specific story event into a **universal moral or practical life principle** applicable beyond the characters (for instance, *"Cooperation and early preparation help communities solve shared problems swiftly"* or *"Honesty and persistence earn long-term respect"*).

Avoid merely retelling plot events (*"Tendai should pick up trash on Tuesday"*)—step one level higher to show the enduring value behind Tendai’s choice, matching the passage’s closing reflection or turning point closely.

ZIMSEC marking guidelines award full credit when you express **one clear moral or practical takeaway** in a crisp full sentence grounded directly in the outcome of the text.

questions.questionText: Which word is closest in meaning to 'responsible' as used in context?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** The word closest in meaning to **"responsible"** as used in context is **"dependable"**, **"trustworthy"**, **"reliable"**, or **"accountable"** (always verify fit by substituting your chosen synonym back into the exact passage sentence to confirm tone and sense stay natural!).

Context-clue strategy works cleanly in three steps: **(1) Read the full sentence before and after "responsible"** to check whether it describes a *trustworthy person* (*"the responsible monitor locked the room"* → **dependable / reliable**) or *causing something* (*"carelessness was responsible for the fire"* → **the cause of / to blame for**). **(2) Match exact part of speech** (adjective ↔ adjective).

Write the exact single-word synonym cleanly rather than writing a whole dictionary paragraph unless asked to *"explain"*—and never write back the word *responsible* inside your definition!

questions.questionText: What does 'they' refer to in the passage?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [1–2 marks]:** Pronoun reference questions asking **"what does 'they' refer to in the passage"** require looking **immediately backward** (earlier in the same sentence or the preceding sentence) to find the **exact plural noun phrase** performing or receiving the action that **"they"** replaces.

Test your answer carefully by plugging that exact plural noun phrase back into the sentence in place of *"they"* (*"[Plural noun group] carried the watering cans..."*)—if the sentence suddenly becomes illogical or singular, look one clause higher! Beware nearby decoy plural nouns (for example *"buckets"* or *"trees"* right beside *"the volunteers"*): check *who* makes sense with the verb!

Give the exact specific plural noun/group from the text cleanly (*"'They' refers to the Grade 7 volunteers / the village committee members"*).

questions.questionText: Why was the activity useful?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** Answering **"why was the activity useful"** directs attention cleanly to the **positive results, outcomes, or improvements** reported in the final two paragraphs—look for result signals like *as a result, consequently, helped, improved, prevented, saved, or succeeded*.

Restate two clear benefits strictly grounded in the text in complete sentences (*"The activity was useful because it cleared clogged drains, stopped classroom flooding, and taught learners hygiene habits"*), rather than inventing unsupported extra benefits like *"everyone became famous."*

Always check how many reasons marks allow ('2 marks' typically expects **two distinct benefits** or one fully explained cause-and-outcome link stated in your own crisp words).

questions.questionText: Which is the best title for the passage?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** Choosing the **best title** requires capturing the passage’s **broad central theme cleanly in 3 to 6 memorable words**—short enough to headline a whole story yet specific enough to exclude unrelated topics (for example: **"Cleaning Up Our Market Together"** rather than vague *"A Busy Day"* or overly narrow *"Brooms and Wheelbarrows"*).

Two quick checks pick winning Paper 2 titles every time: **(1) Read only Paragraph 1 and the last Paragraph**—the strongest title embraces both the starting problem and ending success; **(2) Capitalise major content words neatly** (*Title Case*) without putting a trailing full stop.

Avoid copying a whole 15-word sentence as a title; crisp 3–6-word headlines score instant full marks.

questions.questionText: What happened after the people changed or improved their approach?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** Questions asking **"what happened after the people changed or improved their approach"** trace **direct cause-and-effect contrast** between an early struggle (*before change*) and measurable turnaround (*after change*) inside the passage’s second half.

Locate transition pivots such as *However, Within months, Once they started, After adopting...*, identify the exact visible improvements recorded afterward (for example: *yields doubled, water stayed clear, fewer absences occurred*), and express them cleanly in a full sentence using matching past tense.

Be careful never to describe *what people were doing wrong before the change*—answer strictly what **improved afterward**!

questions.questionText: Which value is most strongly shown?
questions.explanation:
**Comprehension Model Answer & Strategy [2 marks]:** Identifying **"which value is most strongly shown"** looks across characters’ hardest decisions in the text for one unmistakable **Unhu/Ubuntu civic virtue**: such as **honesty** (returning lost money), **teamwork / cooperation** (sharing hard clean-up labour), **perseverance** (refusing to quit after failure), **compassion / empathy**, or **environmental stewardship**.

Name the single strongest **value noun** unmistakably first (*"The value most strongly shown is **honesty**"* or **teamwork**), then back it up briefly with one concrete piece of textual evidence showing characters living out that value when tested.

Stating *both* the precise value name AND its 1-line textual proof locks down full comprehension marks every time.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about reducing household waste. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that households can cut solid waste sharply by avoiding unnecessary single-use plastic packaging, reusing sturdy shopping bags and glass jars, sorting recyclables like cans and bottles from organic peelings, and composting kitchen scraps into rich garden manure instead of burning garbage or dumping litter outdoors.* (47 words.)

Effective **ZIMSEC Grade 7 Summary Writing** follows four strict mechanics: **(1) Start with the exact supplied opening words** (*"The passage explains that..."* counts toward your 50-word total!); **(2) Pack 4–5 distinct factual action verbs** (*avoiding packaging, reusing bags/jars, sorting recyclables, composting scraps, stopping burning/dumping*) into smooth combined sentences instead of long stories; **(3) Keep strictly at or below 50 words**; and **(4) Write in third-person neutral prose** using your own concise phrasing rather than lifting whole wordy sentences.

Examiners cross off every word past word #50 when marking—missing key points at words 51–65! Always count every word cleanly (hyphenated words like *single-use* count as 1 word) and verify smooth grammar with zero repetition.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about preparing for drought. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that communities can prepare effectively for drought by storing harvested rainwater in tanks and sand dams, planting drought-tolerant sorghum and millet alongside early-maturing maize under conservation mulch, protecting dry-season boreholes, and budgeting family grain reserves carefully before harsh dry spells intensify.* (44 words.)

Notice how tight summary phrasing compresses multiple ideas cleanly inside **44 words** (safely under the 50-word ceiling!): **(1) Harvesting/storing water**, **(2) Drought-tolerant crops + mulching**, **(3) Protecting boreholes**, and **(4) Budgeting grain reserves**. Zero unnecessary adjectives, dates, or side examples appear.

In Paper 2 summaries, draw up a quick numbered scratch list of 5 distinct points *before* drafting, join them with clean commas and *"and"*, start verbatim with *"The passage explains that..."*, and recount words carefully before copying your final fair draft.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about benefits of reading. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that regular reading strengthens vocabulary and spelling accuracy, sharpens focus and examination comprehension across every school subject, broadens general knowledge beyond daily life, builds empathy through diverse stories, and offers calm, productive enjoyment while reducing idle screen habits.* (42 words.)

Each phrase captures a clear distinct benefit packed into crisp **parallel verbs** (*strengthens, sharpens, broadens, builds, offers*—42 words total!). Staying cleanly at 42–48 words leaves comfortable safety margin against counting disagreements while hitting every single scoring point on the mark scheme.

Never write bullet lists inside a summary—ZIMSEC requires **one continuous, flowing third-person paragraph** beginning strictly with the mandated opening words.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about safe road use. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that pedestrians stay safe on busy roads by walking facing oncoming traffic on verges, wearing bright reflective colours at dusk, halting completely at designated zebra crossings to look right, left, and right again before stepping off, and never running, playing games, or using earphones near traffic.* (49 words.)

Observe how five concrete lifesaving rules fit cleanly at **49 words** without sacrificing a single detail: facing traffic, high-visibility clothing, Kerb Drill at marked crossings, and avoiding running/distractions. Notice *"look right, left, and right again"* counts accurately in crisp prose.

Watch the exact 50-word limit closely—at 49 words every single word fits inside the ZIMSEC marking cutoff without risking truncation penalties.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about tree conservation. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that learners and villagers conserve trees by planting indigenous and fruit saplings annually, watering and fencing young seedlings against livestock, reporting illegal bush-clearing or wildfires swiftly, reusing paper neatly, and adopting fuel-efficient stoves or solar cooking instead of felling living woodlands.* (44 words.)

All five distinct conservation actions appear cleanly inside **44 words** in continuous third-person grammar starting directly with *"The passage explains that..."*. Combining related points neatly with *"and"* or *"or"* eliminates wordy repetition while guarding clarity.

Avoid wasting summary words on greetings, personal feelings (*"I think trees are lovely"*), or examples repeated twice—stick strictly to verifiable action points.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about healthy school meals. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that nutritious school meals sustain children’s energy and classroom concentration by combining whole grains with body-building beans or kapenta, fresh leafy vegetables, clean boiled or treated drinking water, and strict food-hygiene habits while limiting overly sugary snacks and fizzy drinks.* (44 words.)

Notice how concise summary prose condenses nutritional categories cleanly into **44 words** (carbohydrates/grains + protein beans/fish + vitamins/greens + safe water + hygiene − excess sugar). Every ZIMSEC mark-scheme peg earns instant credit cleanly.

Double-check spelling of key health terms (**nutritious, concentration, vegetables, hygiene**) because ZIMSEC summaries award +1 dedicated Language mark alongside the 4 Content marks.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about managing study time. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that learners manage study time effectively by drafting balanced daily revision timetables, tackling demanding topics when minds are freshest, breaking heavy chapters into short focused sessions with brief rests, eliminating television or phone distractions, and revising consistently ahead of examinations.* (44 words.)

Five clear time-management principles land effortlessly inside **44 words** while retaining lively, grammatically polished verb phrases (*drafting, tackling, breaking, eliminating, revising*). Notice zero first-person *"I/we"* appears anywhere.

Keep an exact final word count below every summary paragraph ('(44 words)') in practice so pacing stays second nature during exam day.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about protecting water sources. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that communities protect vital water sources by siting Blair toilets and livestock kraals well away from wells, maintaining untouched thirty-metre vegetative stream buffers against erosion, banning detergent washing or chemical dumping inside rivers, and sealing borehole aprons cleanly to prevent contamination.* (45 words.)

Five distinct source-protection pillars align cleanly in **45 words**: safe latrine/kraal siting, 30 m stream buffer, preventing washing/chemicals in rivers, and sealing borehole drainage aprons. Clear technical nouns pack deep meaning into minimal words.

Remember never to invent external points absent from the source comprehension text during the exam—filter cleanly for points strictly mentioned in the passage.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about responsible use of technology. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that learners use technology responsibly by harnessing computers and educational apps safely for school research, protecting private passwords and personal addresses online, avoiding harmful cyberbullying or unverified links, and balancing focused daily screen sessions strictly with outdoor exercise, reading, and adequate sleep.* (45 words.)

Five balanced digital-citizenship habits fit neatly inside **45 words**: educational purpose, privacy/passwords, avoiding cyberbullying/unsafe links, and balancing screen time with exercise and sleep.

Always verify you keep the exact opening prompt phrase untouched ('The passage explains that...') and finish cleanly on a complete full-stop sentence.

questions.questionText: In not more than 50 words, summarise the main points about community cooperation. Begin: 'The passage explains that ...'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *The passage explains that community cooperation enables neighbours to finish large tasks—cleaning markets, repairing feeder roads, building clinic shelters, and harvesting crops through traditional nhimbe work—far faster together while lowering household costs, resolving disputes peacefully, and strengthening lasting mutual trust across generations.* (44 words.)

This **44-word** summary unites concrete cooperative projects (*cleaning, road repairs, clinics, nhimbe harvests*) with key social benefits (*speed, lower costs, peace, mutual trust*) in crisp third-person prose.

Checking **content points (4 max) + grammar accuracy (+1)** alongside strictly **≤ 50 words** guarantees full marks across every Grade 7 summary prompt.

questions.questionText: Rewrite in the past tense: 'The learners organise a clean-up campaign every Friday.'
questions.explanation:
**Model Tense Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten cleanly in the **simple past tense**, the sentence becomes: **"The learners organised a clean-up campaign every Friday."** (Or for one completed occasion: *"The learners organised a clean-up campaign last Friday."*) [2 marks]. The regular present verb **"organise"** adds **-d** to become simple past **"organised"** (note ZIMSEC British spelling **organised** with an **s**).

Because simple past tense in English describes actions completed in the past without continuous ongoing time, you alter **only the finite action verb (*organise → organised*)**—do not add *"were"* (*"were organised"* alters into passive meaning!) or keep *"organise"* unchanged. Notice that regular verbs ending already in silent *-e* (*organise, decide, celebrate*) add just **-d**.

Check subject (**The learners**), past verb (**organised**), and object (**a clean-up campaign every Friday.**) word by word to keep full grammar credit.

questions.questionText: Change to reported speech: Tendai said, 'I will finish the work today.'
questions.explanation:
**Model Reported Speech Answer [2 marks]:** Converted correctly into **reported (indirect) speech**, the sentence reads: **"Tendai said that he would finish the work that day."** (Or **"Tendai said that she would finish the work that day."**) [2 marks]. Notice ALL three mandatory ZIMSEC shifts: **(1) pronoun "I" → "he/she"**; **(2) modal verb "will" → "would"**; and **(3) time word "today" → "that day"**, while removing all speech marks and comma.

Mastering reported speech backshifting relies on changing **both verbs and time/place markers** when speech spoken earlier is retold later: *will → would*, *can → could*, *is → was*, *today → that day*, *tomorrow → the next day / the following day*, *yesterday → the day before*, *here → there*.

Leaving **"today"** unchanged ('Tendai said that he would finish the work today') or keeping speech marks ('"he would finish..."') costs 1 full mark immediately in Paper 2 grammar!

questions.questionText: Give the opposite of 'careful' and use it in a sentence.
questions.explanation:
**Model Antonym & Sentence [2 marks]:** The direct opposite (antonym) of **"careful"** is **"careless"** (accept also *reckless* or *negligent*, though **careless** pairs cleanly via *-ful ↔ -less*) [1 mark]. In a clear sentence demonstrating meaning: **"A careless cyclist hit the kerb because he did not watch the turning road ahead."** [1 mark].

Notice how English suffix pairs simplify opposites cleanly: **careful ↔ careless**, **useful ↔ useless**, **helpful ↔ helpless**, **hopeful ↔ hopeless**—each pairs positive presence (*-ful*) against lack (*-less*) while remaining an **adjective** modifying a noun.

Avoid writing weak tautologies like *"A careless person is not careful"*—give a specific everyday action illustrating carelessness cleanly so both the word mark and usage mark are guaranteed.

questions.questionText: Join using 'because': 'The road was wet. The driver slowed down.'
questions.explanation:
**Model Conjunction Answer [2 marks]:** Joined accurately using **"because"**, the sentence becomes: **"The driver slowed down because the road was wet."** (Also grammatically correct: **"Because the road was wet, the driver slowed down."**) [2 marks].

Notice why order matters enormously with **because**: *"because"* MUST introduce the **CAUSE / REASON** (*the road was wet*), NOT the result! Reversing clauses to write *"The road was wet because the driver slowed down"* flips cause and effect backwards and makes zero logical sense—rain wets roads, wet roads cause drivers to slow down!

Check punctuation carefully too: when *because* stands between clauses in the middle, omit the comma; when *Because...* opens the sentence, add a comma after the first clause (*"Because the road was wet, the driver slowed down."*).

questions.questionText: Write the plural of 'community'.
questions.explanation:
**Model Plural Answer [1–2 marks]:** The correct plural spelling of **"community"** is **"communities"** [1 mark]. Rewritten in context: *"Our schools work closely with neighbouring **communities**."*

Look closely at the exact spelling rule governing nouns ending in **-y**: when the letter immediately *before* **-y** is a **consonant** (here **t** in *commun-**it-y***), **drop the -y and add -ies** (**community → communities**, *city → cities*, *library → libraries*, *duty → duties*). By contrast, when a **vowel** precedes **-y** (*boy, day, key*), keep the **y** and add just **-s** (*boys, days, keys*).

Candidates frequently lose spelling marks by writing *"communitys"* or *"communitie's"* (never insert an apostrophe inside an ordinary plural noun!).

questions.questionText: Give one synonym for 'assist'.
questions.explanation:
**Model Synonym Answer [1–2 marks]:** Accurate single-word synonyms for **"assist"** (verb: to give help or support) include **"help"**, **"aid"**, or **"support"** (in context: *"Learners **help / aid** elderly residents carry water containers safely"*) [1 mark].

Always confirm that your synonym shares the **exact same part of speech** as the prompt word: since *"assist"* is an action **verb**, respond with a matching base **verb** (**help / aid / support**) rather than a noun like *"helper"* or *"assistance"*.

Keep answers crisp with one accurate base verb (**help** or **aid**) cleanly matching *"assist"*.

questions.questionText: Identify the adjective: 'The responsible learner reported the danger.'
questions.explanation:
**Model Adjective Identification [1–2 marks]:** The **adjective** in *"The responsible learner reported the danger"* is **"responsible"** [1 mark]. It functions as a describing word (attributive adjective) standing directly before the noun **"learner"**, telling us *what kind of learner* reported the danger.

To spot adjectives reliably in any ZIMSEC sentence, isolate every **noun** first (**learner**, **danger**), then check which modifying words describe colour, size, quality, or character right beside those nouns: **"The"** is a definite article/determiner, **"learner"** is a noun, **"reported"** is the past-tense action verb, **"danger"** is a noun, leaving **"responsible"** unmistakably as the describing adjective.

State **"responsible"** clearly on its own (do not copy whole phrases like *"the responsible learner"*) so the marker sees you isolated the exact word class.

questions.questionText: Punctuate: 'please close the gate said the teacher'
questions.explanation:
**Model Punctuation Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten with exact capital letters, direct speech marks, comma, and full stop, the sentence reads: **"Please close the gate," said the teacher.** [2 marks].

Check all five punctuation edits systematically from left to right: **(1)** Opening quotation marks before **Please**; **(2)** Capital **P** on **Please**; **(3)** A **comma inside closing quotation marks ('gate,"')** separating spoken words from the reporting tag (never a full stop inside 'gate."' before 'said'!); **(4)** Closing quotation marks cleanly after the comma; and **(5)** Lowercase **said** followed by **the teacher.** ending with a **full stop**.

Forgetting either the **comma inside the speech marks (","')** or adding a **period at the very end ('teacher.')** is the #1 ZIMSEC punctuation mistake.

questions.questionText: Change to passive voice: 'The volunteers cleaned the wetland.'
questions.explanation:
**Model Passive Voice Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten cleanly in the **passive voice** preserving the original past tense, the sentence becomes: **"The wetland was cleaned by the volunteers."** [2 marks].

Forming **passive voice** safely follows three crisp steps: **(1) Move the active object (*"The wetland"*) to the front** as the new grammatical subject; **(2) Match auxiliary verb tense + past participle (*cleaned* is simple past, and *"The wetland"* is singular, so use singular past *"was cleaned"*)**; and **(3) Add *"by the volunteers"*** at the end.

Notice two classic passive traps: changing tense wrongly to *"The wetland **is** cleaned"* (wrong present tense!) or using plural *"were cleaned"* beside singular *"wetland"*. Match singular past **was cleaned** cleanly!

questions.questionText: Write the comparative form of 'careful'.
questions.explanation:
**Model Comparative Form Answer [1–2 marks]:** The correct **comparative form** of the three-syllable adjective **"careful"** is **"more careful"** (e.g., *"Tariro is **more careful** than before when crossing busy streets."*) [1 mark]. (The superlative form is *most careful*.)

English comparatives split neatly by syllable count: short one-syllable adjectives add **-er** (*tall → taller, fast → faster*), whereas longer adjectives of two or more syllables ending in *-ful, -ous, -ing*—especially **careful**—take **"more"** in front instead of *-er*! Therefore **"carefuller"** is grammatically incorrect and always penalised.

Double-check never to write double comparatives such as *"more carefuler"* and verify exact single-l spelling (**more careful**).

questions.questionText: Identify the conjunction: 'We stayed inside because the storm was strong.'
questions.explanation:
**Model Conjunction Answer [1–2 marks]:** The **conjunction** linking the two clauses in *"We stayed inside because the storm was strong"* is **"because"** [1 mark]. It functions as a **subordinating conjunction of reason**, joining the main action clause (*"We stayed inside"*) smoothly to its explanation (*"the storm was strong"*).

To locate conjunctions rapidly, find the two complete mini-sentences (*"We stayed inside"* + *"the storm was strong"*) and circle the single joining word standing directly between them (**because**, *and, but, although, while, since*).

Write **"because"** cleanly on its own rather than copying the whole clause after it.

questions.questionText: Replace 'very tired' with a stronger single word.
questions.explanation:
**Model Stronger Vocabulary Answer [1–2 marks]:** Accurate single words replacing the weak phrase **"very tired"** include **"exhausted"**, **"fatigued"**, **"weary"**, or **"worn"** (best choice in ZIMSEC Grade 7 essays: **"exhausted"**—e.g., *"After the long hill climb, the hikers felt completely **exhausted**."*) [1 mark].

Precise vocabulary elevates descriptive compositions immediately because a single vivid adjective (**exhausted**, *furious* instead of *very angry*, *freezing* instead of *very cold*, *enormous* instead of *very big*) sounds sharp and expressive without needing weak intensifiers like *"very"*.

Check spelling carefully (**ex-haus-ted**—mind the silent **h**!) and respond strictly with **one single strong adjective**.

questions.questionText: Write the possessive form of 'the teachers books'.
questions.explanation:
**Model Possessive Apostrophe Answer [2 marks]:** Since *"teachers"* ends in **-s** as a **plural noun** representing more than one teacher owning the books, place the apostrophe **cleanly after the s**: **"the teachers' books"** [2 marks]. (Contrast singular ownership for just one teacher: *the **teacher’s** book*.)

Possessive apostrophe placement depends strictly on **whether the owner is singular or plural**: **(1)** One owner (*one boy, one teacher*) adds **'s** (*the teacher's books*); **(2)** Plural owners ending already in **-s** (*many teachers, all learners*) add **ONLY '''** after the final **s** (*the teachers' books*, *the learners' uniforms*); **(3)** Irregular plurals not ending in -s (*children, women*) add **'s** (*the children's books*).

Notice the prompt already prints *"the teachers books"* with plural **teachers**, making **the teachers’ books** exact!

questions.questionText: Change into a statement: 'Did the learners finish the project?'
questions.explanation:
**Model Statement Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten cleanly from an interrogative question into a declarative **statement**, the sentence reads: **"The learners finished the project."** [2 marks].

Notice why **"Did ... finish"** merges back into **"finished"**: in English question formation, simple past statements hide no auxiliary—instead, forming a question pulls *"Did"* to the front and resets the main verb to base *"finish"*. Turning it back into a statement **drops "Did"**, restores past tense **"-ed" ('finished')** onto the main verb, puts **"The learners"** first, and swaps the '?' question mark for a crisp **'.' full stop**!

Leaving '"The learners did finish"' sounds needlessly emphatic and often loses a point in standard transformation tasks—and forgetting the **full stop '.'** or mistakenly keeping **finish** (*"The learners finish the project"*) costs marks too.

questions.questionText: Use the idiom 'once in a blue moon' correctly in a sentence.
questions.explanation:
**Model Idiom Sentence [2 marks]:** A clear, context-rich sentence using **"once in a blue moon"** correctly is: **"My busy cousin lives overseas and visits our village in Masvingo only once in a blue moon, so we throw a joyful welcome feast whenever he arrives."** [2 marks].

The idiom **"once in a blue moon"** means **very rarely / almost never / on exceedingly rare occasions** (originating from rare extra full moons occurring within a calendar season). Notice how your sentence must include a clear **clue proving rarity** (e.g., *"lives overseas"*, *"rarely happens"*): writing *"We go to school once in a blue moon"* contradicts everyday truth or sounds vague without context!

Always make sure the context around any ZIMSEC idiom proves clearly to the examiner that you understand its figurative meaning.
